title: Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics
goal: By the end you can say what the key-value model answers and where it stops, store and read payments in DynamoDB with the Kotlin Enhanced Client, make a payment create idempotent with a conditional write, and read an account's newest payments with one Query.

warmup.q: A consumer sends DynamoDB a `PutItem` for a payment, the call times out, and the consumer sends the exact same `PutItem` again. The first call had in fact succeeded. What is in the table now?
options: Two items, one for each PutItem
One item: the second PutItem replaced the first without an error
One item, and the second PutItem failed with a duplicate-key error
Nothing: DynamoDB rolls back a request whose caller timed out
warmup.why: PutItem replaces any item with the same primary key, silently, so an identical retry leaves one item. Only a condition expression makes the second write fail. And if the item's key had contained the arrival time, the retry would have built a new key and you'd have two items: that's the trap this lesson is about.

sections.h: DynamoDB is a hash map of small sorted maps
sections.body:
Lesson 2 turned questions into keys. Now build the simplest store a key can serve, and see the one idea that makes it fit payments. You want two things from a payments store. Fetch one payment by its key in a few milliseconds, and list an account's newest payments, whether the table holds 50 million payments or 5 billion, without running database servers yourself.

Start with the simplest store that could work: a key-value store. It has two operations, `put(key, value)` and `get(key)`. It hashes the key to choose a partition, one slice of the data held by a few machines, so both operations cost the same however big the table grows. Redis is the in-memory example, with its own track. Amazon DynamoDB is a managed, durable one: AWS runs the machines, and each partition keeps copies in several availability zones (separate data centres in one AWS Region), with one copy acting as leader, as lesson 1 described.

A pure key-value store answers the first question and fails the second. "A-1001's newest payments" isn't one key, and the store can't see inside its values, so it would have to read everything. Stonebraker and Pavlo's 2024 survey makes the same point about the whole family: as soon as a value has several fields, the application has to parse it, and every secondary lookup is code you write. That's why DynamoDB, like Aerospike, grew into a store of records with named attributes. DynamoDB adds one idea that fixes this, and it's easiest to see on a real item. An item is the unit DynamoDB stores. Here is one, the way the API sends it:

```json
{
  "pk":          { "S": "ACCT#A-1001" },
  "sk":          { "S": "PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:03.120Z#pay-81723" },
  "amountMinor": { "N": "4250" },
  "currency":    { "S": "EUR" }
}
```

Each attribute has a name and a typed value: `S` for a string, `N` for a number (sent as text, so no precision is lost), and also binary, lists, maps and sets. An item can be at most 400 KB. When you create a table you declare only the primary key; every other attribute is up to each item.

This table's primary key has two attributes. `pk` is the partition key: DynamoDB hashes it to pick the partition, so it only ever answers "equals". `sk` is the sort key: DynamoDB stores all items with the same `pk` together, sorted by `sk`. That sorted group is an item collection. **The picture for this lesson is a hash map from partition key to a small sorted map.** It's lesson 1's two answers in one table: hash to place the data, sort to make ranges cheap. The `ACCT#` and `PAY#` prefixes let different kinds of item share one collection, which lesson 4 builds on. A table can also have a simple key, the partition key alone, where each value names exactly one item.

DynamoDB meters capacity by item size, so real sizes matter. A read unit covers one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent reads. A write unit covers one write per second of up to 1 KB. So a 300-byte payment costs one write unit to write and half a read unit to read. Each partition tops out at 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, so a partition key everyone writes to, like one huge merchant on Black Friday, hits a ceiling whatever the table's settings say. Big items reach it sooner: a 400 KB item costs 400 write units, so one partition takes about 2.5 such writes a second. The Partitioning track's lesson on hot keys spreads that load.

Reads are eventually consistent by default: any copy may answer, including one that hasn't yet received a write that finished moments ago. They cost half. Set `ConsistentRead` to true and the leader answers, so you see every write that has succeeded. Global secondary indexes, the extra copies from lesson 2, can't do strongly consistent reads at all.

try.title: Look inside an item collection
steps: From the `labs` folder, start DynamoDB Local 3.3.2: `docker compose -f env/dynamodb.yml up -d`. It runs in memory on port 8000 and accepts any credentials. Leave it running for this lesson's other Try-its.

Read `ItemCollectionDemo.kt`. It creates a table, then writes five items in a scrambled order: four for account A-1001 and one for A-2002. Predict the order in which the Query prints A-1001's sort keys.

code.title: ItemCollectionDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
Query pk = ACCT#A-1001:
  META
  PAY#2026-11-06T18:40:51.004Z#pay-80911
  PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:03.120Z#pay-81723
  REFUND#2026-11-07T11:02:00.000Z#ref-12
GetItem (ACCT#A-1001, META): {sk=AttributeValue(S=META), customerId=AttributeValue(S=C-77), currency=AttributeValue(S=EUR), pk=AttributeValue(S=ACCT#A-1001)}
```

DynamoDB returns the item collection in sort-key order (UTF-8 bytes): `M` < `P` < `R`, so META, then the payments in time order, then the refund. A-2002's item never appears, because a Query reads one partition. GetItem needs both key attributes and prints the raw item: a map of typed `AttributeValue`s. The map's printed order can differ on your machine; it's a hash map.

sections.h: The Enhanced Client maps a Kotlin class to an item
sections.body:
The item above, built in code, is a `Map<String, AttributeValue>` with a typed wrapper around every value. That's what `DynamoDbClient`, the low-level client in the AWS SDK for Java 2.x, makes you write, and the demo in the previous section does exactly that. You'd rather write a Kotlin class and let a library convert it. The Enhanced Client is that library, built on top of the low-level client. AWS describes it as the successor to the `DynamoDBMapper` of SDK v1.

You reach DynamoDB Local with the normal client and an endpoint override, which points the client at your laptop instead of AWS. Any credentials work locally, but the SDK insists on having some, and on a Region:

```kotlin
val low = DynamoDbClient.builder()
    .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000"))
    .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
    .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz")))
    .build()
val enhanced = DynamoDbEnhancedClient.builder().dynamoDbClient(low).build()
```

The simplest mapping comes from a bean: a class with a no-argument constructor plus a getter and setter per property. A Kotlin data class doesn't have that shape, so use a plain class with `var` properties and default values. The key annotations must sit on the getter, which is what the `@get:` prefix does:

```kotlin
@DynamoDbBean
class PaymentItem {
    @get:DynamoDbPartitionKey
    var pk: String = ""

    @get:DynamoDbSortKey
    var sk: String = ""

    var paymentId: String = ""
    var amountMinor: Long = 0     // cents: no Double near money
    var createdAt: String = ""
}

val payments = enhanced.table("payments", TableSchema.fromBean(PaymentItem::class.java))
payments.putItem(item)
val back = payments.getItem(Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-1001").sortValue(item.sk).build())
```

If you'd rather keep immutable classes, the Enhanced Client also supports `@DynamoDbImmutable` classes with a builder, and `StaticTableSchema` for a schema written in code. The lab maps two classes, `PaymentItem` and `IdempotencyItem`, onto one table: the Enhanced Client only needs each class's key attributes to match the table's.

One behaviour of `putItem` matters for payments. If an item with the same primary key already exists, PutItem replaces it. No error, no warning, and the old attributes are gone. The next section turns that into a problem, then into a tool.

sections.h: Make the create idempotent with one conditional write
sections.body:
Payment creates get retried. A Kafka consumer is handed a message again after a rebalance (a reshuffle of which consumer reads which partition of a topic). A Temporal activity times out after its write landed, and runs again. An HTTP client gives up on a create that waited on a 120 ms card-issuer call, and retries. Each retry carries the same request, and none of them may create a second payment.

So the client marks every request with an idempotency key: a value it generates once per logical request, often a UUID, and sends again on every retry. The store must make sure each key creates at most one payment. Build that up.

Version 1 checks, then writes: `GetItem` the key, and if nothing comes back, `PutItem` the payment. Now two consumers handle the same redelivered message 2 ms apart. Both `GetItem` calls run before either `PutItem`, both see nothing, and both create a payment. Checking and then acting in two separate requests is a race whenever two callers can run at once.

Version 2 writes a claim item whose key comes from the idempotency key, `pk = IDEMP#9f1c` and `sk = IDEMP`, so both consumers write the same item. But a plain `PutItem` replaces an existing item without a word. Both writes succeed, both consumers believe they won, and both go on to create a payment.

Version 3 adds a condition expression. **A write can carry a condition, and DynamoDB checks it against the target item and applies the write in one step:**

```kotlin
val unclaimed = Expression.builder()
    .expression("attribute_not_exists(pk) OR expiresAt < :now")
    .putExpressionValue(":now", AttributeValue.fromN(now.toString()))
    .build()
claims.putItem(
    PutItemEnhancedRequest.builder(IdempotencyItem::class.java)
        .item(claim)                       // pk = IDEMP#<key>, sk = IDEMP
        .conditionExpression(unclaimed)
        .build()
)
```

`attribute_not_exists(pk)` is true only when no item with this exact primary key exists. If the condition is false, DynamoDB writes nothing and throws `ConditionalCheckFailedException`, and it still charges the write units. The loser then reads the claim and returns the first payment's id, so every caller gets the same answer. The condition only works if every retry builds the same key. Put the arrival time or a fresh UUID into the claim's key, and each retry writes a new item that the condition never sees.

Version 4 makes claims expire. They can't live forever: at 2,000 creates a second, one day adds about 173 million claims. So each claim stores `expiresAt`, a Number of Unix epoch seconds (seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC), and you turn on TTL (time to live) for that attribute. DynamoDB then deletes expired items in the background, typically within a few days of expiry, without charging write units. Until then the expired claim is still in the table, which is why the condition also accepts `expiresAt < :now`.

One gap is left. The claim and the payment are two separate writes. If the process dies between them, a retry finds the claim and reports a payment that was never written. Lesson 4 closes that gap with `TransactWriteItems`, DynamoDB's call for writing several items all or nothing.

try.title: Write the same payment three ways
steps: With DynamoDB Local still running, read `ConditionalPutDemo.kt`. It writes the same payment twice in three ways: a plain put, a conditional put, and a conditional put whose sort key holds the arrival time.
For each way, predict: does the second write fail, and how many items end up in the table?

code.title: ConditionalPutDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.model.l03.demo

import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.StaticCredentialsProvider
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.DynamoDbEnhancedClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.Expression
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.Key
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.TableSchema
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.mapper.annotations.DynamoDbBean
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.mapper.annotations.DynamoDbPartitionKey
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.mapper.annotations.DynamoDbSortKey
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.model.PutItemEnhancedRequest
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.model.QueryConditional
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.DynamoDbClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ConditionalCheckFailedException
import java.net.URI

/** A Kotlin class the Enhanced Client can map: var properties with defaults, key annotations on the getters. */
@DynamoDbBean
class DemoPayment {
    @get:DynamoDbPartitionKey
    var pk: String = ""

    @get:DynamoDbSortKey
    var sk: String = ""

    var amountMinor: Long = 0
}

/** Three ways to write "the same" payment twice. Only one of them notices. */
fun main() {
    val low = DynamoDbClient.builder()
        .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000"))
        .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
        .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz")))
        .build()
    val enhanced = DynamoDbEnhancedClient.builder().dynamoDbClient(low).build()
    val table = enhanced.table("demo-conditional", TableSchema.fromBean(DemoPayment::class.java))
    runCatching { table.deleteTable() } // start clean on every run
    table.createTable()

    fun payment(pk: String, sk: String, amount: Long) =
        DemoPayment().apply { this.pk = pk; this.sk = sk; amountMinor = amount }
    val key = Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-1001").sortValue("PAY#pay-81723").build()

    // 1. plain PutItem twice with the same key: the second silently replaces the first
    table.putItem(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-81723", 4250))
    table.putItem(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-81723", 9900))
    println("1. plain put twice: no error, amountMinor is now ${table.getItem(key).amountMinor}")

    // 2. the same write with a condition: only if no item with this key exists yet
    val mustBeNew = Expression.builder().expression("attribute_not_exists(pk)").build()
    fun putIfNew(item: DemoPayment) = table.putItem(
        PutItemEnhancedRequest.builder(DemoPayment::class.java).item(item).conditionExpression(mustBeNew).build()
    )
    putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-90001", 4250))
    println("2. conditional put of pay-90001: written")
    try {
        putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-90001", 4250))
    } catch (e: ConditionalCheckFailedException) {
        println("   again: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.awsErrorDetails().errorMessage()}")
    }

    // 3. the trap: the sort key contains the ARRIVAL time, and the retry arrives 3 seconds later
    putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-2002", "PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:03.120Z", 4250))
    putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-2002", "PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:06.480Z", 4250))
    val copies = table.query(QueryConditional.keyEqualTo(Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-2002").build()))
        .items().count()
    println("3. retry with a time-based key: both conditional puts succeeded, A-2002 now has $copies payments")
    low.close()
}

try.expect:
```text
1. plain put twice: no error, amountMinor is now 9900
2. conditional put of pay-90001: written
   again: ConditionalCheckFailedException: The conditional request failed
3. retry with a time-based key: both conditional puts succeeded, A-2002 now has 2 payments
```

Case 1 is the silent overwrite: the second put wins and nobody is told. Case 2 is the fix: same key, so the second write is refused. Case 3 is the trap. The condition worked exactly as written, but the retry built a different key, so there was nothing for it to find, and the account now shows the payment twice.

sections.h: Read a range with Query, not with Scan
sections.body:
`GetItem` needs the whole primary key, both `pk` and `sk`. For "A-1001's 20 newest payments" you know the partition key but none of the sort keys. `Scan` would read every item in the table. `Query` is the read made for an item collection.

A Query must give the partition key with `=`. It may add one condition on the sort key: `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `BETWEEN` or `begins_with`. DynamoDB goes to the partition, finds the first matching item in sort order and reads forward, or backward when you set `ScanIndexForward` to false. AP1 from lesson 2 is one Query:

```kotlin
val onlyPayments = QueryConditional.sortBeginsWith(
    Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-1001").sortValue("PAY#").build()
)
val newest = payments.query(
    QueryEnhancedRequest.builder()
        .queryConditional(onlyPayments)
        .scanIndexForward(false)   // newest first
        .limit(20)                 // DynamoDB stops after 20 items
        .build()
).items().take(20)                 // and Kotlin stops asking for pages
```

`begins_with(sk, "PAY#")` keeps the read to payments: `META` sorts before them and refunds sort after them. Reading backward starts at the newest.

Results come in pages. One Query call returns at most 1 MB, counted before any filter. If there's more, the response carries `LastEvaluatedKey`, and the next call starts from there. The Enhanced Client's `items()` follows the pages for you, lazily.

Two other tools look similar and cost far more. A `FilterExpression` runs after the read, so a Query with a filter pays for every item in its run and returns only some of them. A `Scan` reads the whole table, page by page. Keep Scan for exports and backfills, and never put one on a request path.

String sort keys sort by UTF-8 bytes, so a timestamp inside a key must be fixed width and in one time zone. `Instant.toString()` drops zero milliseconds, which makes `10:15:03Z` sort after `10:15:03.120Z`, because `Z` comes after `.` in byte order. The lab formats every time as `yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'` for that reason.

try.title: Compare what Query, a filter and Scan read
steps: With DynamoDB Local still running, read `QueryCostDemo.kt`. It writes 2,000 payments for 100 accounts, 20 each, then asks for account A-0042's payments three ways, with `ReturnConsumedCapacity` turned on.
Predict, for each way, how many items DynamoDB reads to return what was asked for.
Run it. Then stop DynamoDB Local: `docker compose -f env/dynamodb.yml down -v`.

code.title: QueryCostDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.model.l03.demo

import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.StaticCredentialsProvider
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.DynamoDbClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.AttributeDefinition
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.AttributeValue
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.BillingMode
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.KeySchemaElement
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.KeyType
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.PutRequest
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ReturnConsumedCapacity
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ScalarAttributeType
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.WriteRequest
import java.net.URI
import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneOffset
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter

/** 2,000 payments for 100 accounts. Three ways to find one account's payments, and what each one reads. */
fun main() {
    val ddb = DynamoDbClient.builder()
        .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000"))
        .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
        .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz")))
        .build()
    val table = "demo-query-cost"
    runCatching { ddb.deleteTable { it.tableName(table) } }
    ddb.createTable {
        it.tableName(table)
            .attributeDefinitions(
                AttributeDefinition.builder().attributeName("pk").attributeType(ScalarAttributeType.S).build(),
                AttributeDefinition.builder().attributeName("sk").attributeType(ScalarAttributeType.S).build(),
            )
            .keySchema(
                KeySchemaElement.builder().attributeName("pk").keyType(KeyType.HASH).build(),
                KeySchemaElement.builder().attributeName("sk").keyType(KeyType.RANGE).build(),
            )
            .billingMode(BillingMode.PAY_PER_REQUEST)
    }

    // seed: account A-0000 .. A-0099, 20 payments each, amounts 500..10,000 cents
    val fmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'").withZone(ZoneOffset.UTC)
    val start = Instant.parse("2026-11-01T00:00:00Z")
    val items = (0 until 2_000).map { i ->
        val account = "A-%04d".format(i % 100)
        val at = fmt.format(start.plusSeconds(i * 157L))
        mapOf(
            "pk" to s("ACCT#$account"), "sk" to s("PAY#$at#pay-$i"),
            "accountId" to s(account), "amountMinor" to n(500L + (i * 7919L) % 9_501),
        )
    }
    items.chunked(25).forEach { batch -> // BatchWriteItem takes at most 25 items
        ddb.batchWriteItem { it.requestItems(mapOf(table to batch.map { item ->
            WriteRequest.builder().putRequest(PutRequest.builder().item(item).build()).build()
        })) }
    }

    // A. Query: one partition, one range, read from the end
    val a = ddb.query {
        it.tableName(table)
            .keyConditionExpression("pk = :pk AND begins_with(sk, :pay)")
            .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":pk" to s("ACCT#A-0042"), ":pay" to s("PAY#")))
            .scanIndexForward(false).limit(5)
            .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL)
    }
    println("A. Query, newest 5:          returned %4d, read %4d, capacity units %s".format(a.count(), a.scannedCount(), a.consumedCapacity()?.capacityUnits()))
    a.items().take(2).forEach { println("     ${it["sk"]!!.s()}") }

    // B. Query plus a filter: the filter runs AFTER the read
    val b = ddb.query {
        it.tableName(table)
            .keyConditionExpression("pk = :pk")
            .filterExpression("amountMinor > :big")
            .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":pk" to s("ACCT#A-0042"), ":big" to n(8_000)))
            .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL)
    }
    println("B. Query + filter > 80.00:   returned %4d, read %4d, capacity units %s".format(b.count(), b.scannedCount(), b.consumedCapacity()?.capacityUnits()))

    // C. Scan with a filter on a non-key attribute: reads the whole table to find 20 items
    val c = ddb.scanPaginator {
        it.tableName(table)
            .filterExpression("accountId = :acct")
            .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":acct" to s("A-0042")))
            .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL)
    }.toList()
    println("C. Scan + filter on account: returned %4d, read %4d, capacity units %s".format(
        c.sumOf { it.count() }, c.sumOf { it.scannedCount() }, c.sumOf { it.consumedCapacity()?.capacityUnits() ?: 0.0 }))
    ddb.close()
}

private fun s(v: String): AttributeValue = AttributeValue.fromS(v)
private fun n(v: Long): AttributeValue = AttributeValue.fromN(v.toString())

try.expect:
```text
A. Query, newest 5:          returned    5, read    5, capacity units 0.5
     PAY#2026-11-04T12:41:34.000Z#pay-1942
     PAY#2026-11-04T08:19:54.000Z#pay-1842
B. Query + filter > 80.00:   returned    4, read   20, capacity units 0.5
C. Scan + filter on account: returned   20, read 2000, capacity units 20.0
```

`read` is DynamoDB's `ScannedCount` and `returned` is `Count`. The Query reads exactly what it returns, newest first. The filter in B reads all 20 of the account's items to return 4, so it costs the same as reading all 20. The Scan reads all 2,000 items to return 20 and costs 40 times as much as the Query. At 50 million payments it would read 50 million.

refs.title: Key condition expressions for the Query operation

analogy: A DynamoDB table works like the safe-deposit room of a bank. The partition key is the box number: the clerk walks straight to the box, however many boxes the room holds. Inside each box, documents are filed in order of the label on their tab (the sort key), so "everything labelled PAY, from the back, the last 20" is a quick flip. A conditional write is the clerk refusing to file a document when one with the same tab is already in the box. A Scan is asking the clerk to open every box in the room to find documents that mention one merchant. The analogy breaks on size: a real box is a fixed size, while DynamoDB splits a busy or growing partition behind your back, and the room only stays fast if many different box numbers are in use, so no single clerk does all the work.
in_your_world: Your payments API most likely keeps idempotency keys in Oracle with a unique constraint and inserts the key before it charges the card. That's the same idea as `attribute_not_exists`: let the store reject the second writer. The DynamoDB version earns its keep in the Kafka consumers that turn authorizations into account views. Each consumer instance claims the message's idempotency key with a conditional put, so a rebalance that redelivers a batch costs a few failed conditions instead of duplicate payments. In Temporal, put the conditional write inside the activity, not the workflow: a retried activity then hits the condition instead of writing twice.
mistake: The most common mistake is putting the arrival time, or a freshly generated UUID, into the key of the item that is supposed to stop duplicates. Each retry then builds a different key, `attribute_not_exists(pk)` checks an item that doesn't exist, and every retry succeeds. People do it because "put a timestamp in the sort key" is good advice for the payment item itself, and the two keys get mixed up. The fix: the claim's key comes only from the client's idempotency key. The time goes in an attribute, and into the payment item's sort key, which is written only after the claim succeeds.

compare.title: One conditional put, two clients

a.label: DynamoDbClient: raw items
a.src:
// every value is a typed AttributeValue; numbers travel as strings
low.putItem { r ->
    r.tableName("payments")
        .item(mapOf(
            "pk" to AttributeValue.fromS("IDEMP#9f1c"),
            "sk" to AttributeValue.fromS("IDEMP"),
            "paymentId" to AttributeValue.fromS("pay-81723"),
            "expiresAt" to AttributeValue.fromN("1794132000"),
        ))
        .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk) OR expiresAt < :now")
        .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":now" to AttributeValue.fromN("1794045600")))
}

b.label: Enhanced Client: a mapped class

compare.note: Both send the same PutItem request with the same condition string. The Enhanced Client maps your object to attributes; it doesn't hide the API, so conditions, keys and pages work the same way. The raw client is handy in tooling and tests, where you want to see exactly what's stored. The Enhanced Client keeps service code typed. Either way, `ConditionalCheckFailedException` is the signal that someone else's item is already there.

worked.title: Trace a retried payment through createPayment

steps.say: A request arrives at 10:00:00 UTC with idempotency key `9f1c` and payment id `pay-81723`. `createPayment` builds the claim. Its key comes only from the idempotency key; the time goes into `expiresAt`.
steps.code:
val now = cmd.at.epochSecond                       // 1794045600
val claim = IdempotencyItem().apply {
    pk = claimKey(cmd.idempotencyKey)             // IDEMP#9f1c
    sk = CLAIM_SORT_KEY                           // IDEMP
    paymentId = cmd.paymentId                     // pay-81723
    fingerprint = cmd.fingerprint()               // A-1001|M-0042|4250|EUR
    expiresAt = now + CLAIM_TTL_SECONDS           // 1794132000
}

steps.say: The conditional put succeeds, so the store writes the payment item next. The table now holds two items in two partitions.
steps.code:
pk            sk                                       attributes
IDEMP#9f1c    IDEMP                                    paymentId=pay-81723, expiresAt=1794132000
ACCT#A-1001   PAY#2026-11-07T10:00:00.000Z#pay-81723   amountMinor=4250, status=AUTHORIZED

steps.say: The client's HTTP call timed out, so it retries 3 seconds later with the same key and body. The claim's key is identical, the condition finds the live item, and DynamoDB throws. The catch block reads the claim with a strongly consistent read and compares fingerprints.

Two more cases, both covered by the lab's tests. The same key with a different amount is a `Mismatch`: your API should reject it, not hand back the old payment. And 25 hours later the claim has expired. TTL may not have deleted it yet, but `expiresAt < :now` is true, so the key can be used again.
steps.code:
retry, same body, 3 s later    -> Replayed(pay-81723)   nothing written
same key, amount 9900          -> Mismatch(pay-81723)   nothing written
same key, 25 hours later       -> Created(pay-2)        claim replaced

lab.title: Store payments in DynamoDB Local, once per idempotency key
steps: Docker must be running. The tests start DynamoDB Local 3.3.2 through Testcontainers (the first run pulls the image) and give every test its own table. You don't need the Compose service for the lab.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All seven fail with `NotImplementedError`.
Read `PaymentItems.kt`. It holds the two item classes that share one table, the request and the three possible results. Nothing to change there.
Write `recentPayments` in `PaymentStore.kt` as one Query: `begins_with` on `PAY#`, `scanIndexForward(false)`, a limit. Two tests pass.
Write `createPayment`: the conditional put of the claim, then the payment, and the catch block that reads the claim and compares fingerprints. All seven pass.
Run the tests three more times. The concurrency test fires eight identical requests at once, and it must pass every time.
hints: `payments.query(request).items()` is an `Iterable` that fetches pages lazily, so `.take(limit)` returns a `List` and stops asking for pages.
Expression values are typed: `.putExpressionValue(":now", AttributeValue.fromN(now.toString()))`. Numbers travel as strings.
A strongly consistent read with the Enhanced Client: `claims.getItem { r -> r.key(key); r.consistentRead(true) }`.
If the retry test finds two payment items, your claim's key isn't built from the idempotency key alone.
lab.done_when: All seven tests in `PaymentStoreTest` pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: The claim's conditional put from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. Write the Kotlin that puts an `IdempotencyItem` named `claim` into the table `claims`, only if no live claim exists (none at all, or one whose `expiresAt` is before `now`), and returns `true` if this caller won and `false` if someone else holds the key.

recap: DynamoDB hashes the partition key to pick a partition and keeps items with the same partition key together, sorted by the sort key: an item collection.
Capacity is per item size: a read unit covers 4 KB, a write unit 1 KB, and one partition tops out at 3,000 reads and 1,000 writes a second.
PutItem silently replaces an item with the same key. A condition expression such as `attribute_not_exists(pk)` makes the check and the write one atomic step on that item.
An idempotency claim's key must come from the idempotency key alone. TTL deletes expired items lazily, so the condition must also accept an expired claim.
Query reads one partition, optionally one sort-key range, forward or backward, up to 1 MB per page. Filters run after the read; Scan reads the whole table.

quiz.q: A table has keys `pk` and `sk`. You `PutItem` the key (`ACCT#A-1001`, `PAY#...#pay-81723`) with `attribute_not_exists(pk)`. An item with the same `pk` but a different `sk` already exists. What happens?
options: The write succeeds: the condition looks only at the item with this exact pk and sk
The write fails, because `pk` already exists in the partition
The write fails with a validation error, because `pk` always exists
The write succeeds and replaces the other item in the partition
quiz.why: DynamoDB evaluates a condition against the single item named by the request's full primary key. No item has this pk and sk, so `attribute_not_exists(pk)` is true. Other items in the same partition don't matter, and a put never touches an item with a different key.

quiz.q: An account has 20 payments. A Query on its partition with `FilterExpression amountMinor > 8000` returns 4 items. What did it read?
options: 4 items, because the filter is applied inside the index
Every item in the table
All 20 of the account's items; the filter dropped 16 after reading them
Nothing until the filter matched, then 4 items
quiz.why: A filter runs after the Query reads its slice, so you pay for all 20 items and get 4. That's why `ScannedCount` and `Count` differ. It isn't a table scan, though: the key condition still limits the read to one partition.

quiz.q: A claim's `expiresAt` passed two hours ago. TTL is on for that attribute. What does a GetItem for the claim return now?
options: Nothing: TTL deletes an item the moment it expires
Possibly the item: TTL deletes typically within a few days, so check `expiresAt` yourself
An error saying the item has expired
The item, but with every attribute except the key removed
quiz.why: TTL deletion is a background process that typically runs within a few days of expiry. Until then the item is a normal item, which is why the lab's condition treats `expiresAt < :now` as free and why AWS suggests filtering expired items out of reads.

quiz.q: Which of these reads can be strongly consistent?
options: A Query on a global secondary index with `ConsistentRead` true
A GetItem on the table with `ConsistentRead` true
Any read on a table in on-demand mode
A read from DynamoDB Streams
quiz.why: Tables and local secondary indexes support strongly consistent reads. Global secondary indexes and streams are always eventually consistent, because they're updated asynchronously from the table. The capacity mode doesn't change consistency.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: a payments table has partition key `accountId` and sort key `createdAt`. Support now needs merchant M-0042's FAILED payments for any time window, many times an hour. What's the right fix?
options: Scan the table with a FilterExpression on merchantId and status
Query every account's partition and filter by merchant
Add `createdAt` to the partition key
Add a global secondary index keyed by merchantId, with status then createdAt in the sort key
quiz.why: A new access pattern on a hot path needs a key that answers it. With the merchant as partition key and status before time in the sort key, `status = FAILED` fixes a prefix and the time window is one slice. Scans and per-account fan-out cost in proportion to the table, and changing the table's partition key breaks AP1.

flashcards.front: What does DynamoDB PutItem do when an item with the same key exists?
flashcards.back: Replaces it, silently. Add a condition expression if you want the second write refused.

flashcards.front: What does `attribute_not_exists(pk)` check in a PutItem?
flashcards.back: Whether the one item named by this request's full primary key exists. Not the rest of the partition.

flashcards.front: What happens when a condition expression is false?
flashcards.back: Nothing is written, DynamoDB throws `ConditionalCheckFailedException`, and the write units are still charged.

flashcards.front: TTL: what format, and how fast?
flashcards.back: A Number attribute of Unix epoch seconds. Expired items are deleted in the background, typically within a few days, at no write cost.

flashcards.front: One read unit and one write unit cover what?
flashcards.back: Read: one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB (or two eventually consistent). Write: one write per second of up to 1 KB.

flashcards.front: How much does one Query call return at most?
flashcards.back: 1 MB, measured before any filter. `LastEvaluatedKey` in the response means there are more pages.

flashcards.front: How do you write an Enhanced Client bean in Kotlin?
flashcards.back: `@DynamoDbBean` on a class with `var` properties and defaults; key annotations on the getters: `@get:DynamoDbPartitionKey`, `@get:DynamoDbSortKey`.

terms.plain: One record in a DynamoDB table: a set of typed attributes, at most 400 KB.
All items with the same partition key, stored together and sorted by sort key.
A test DynamoDB checks against the target item in the same step as the write; if it's false, nothing is written.
A value the client sends with a request so that repeats of the request are recognised and do nothing new.
A Number attribute of epoch seconds after which DynamoDB deletes the item in the background.
DynamoDB's metering: a read unit covers 4 KB read strongly consistently, a write unit covers 1 KB written.
The AWS SDK for Java 2.x layer that maps your classes to DynamoDB items and back.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why `if (table.getItem(key) == null) table.putItem(item)` doesn't make payment creation idempotent in DynamoDB, and what does.
explain_back.answer: It's check-then-act across two requests. Two consumers handling the same redelivered message can both run the GetItem before either runs the PutItem, so both see nothing and both write. A plain PutItem never complains about an existing item, it replaces it, so nothing stops the second writer. What works is putting the check inside the write: a PutItem with a condition such as `attribute_not_exists(pk)`. DynamoDB evaluates the condition and applies the write as one step on that item, so exactly one caller wins and the others get `ConditionalCheckFailedException`. The losers then read the winning claim and return its payment id. Two more things matter: the claim's key must be built from the idempotency key only, so every retry targets the same item, and an expired claim must count as free, because TTL deletes lazily.
